title: Getting Better Never Stops
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison sets out how curriculum leaders in high-performing departments respond to exam results with a disciplined four-stage cycle of diagnose, treat, assess and review. He argues that the best leaders resist jumping to solutions and instead triangulate evidence such as question-level analysis, recalled scripts, staff sitting the paper, mock data, book scrutiny and lesson visits to find root causes rather than symptoms. Treatment should be limited to two or three highly specific priorities, supported by targeted professional development and a sense of shared ownership across the team. Allison stresses that many departments skip the assessment stage, so leaders must define in advance what evidence would show a change is working and check implementation fidelity. The piece closes with the habits that distinguish outstanding curriculum leaders, including keeping the five-year curriculum central and treating results analysis as the start of improvement rather than its end.
points: Good diagnosis asks exactly where attainment fell short and for whom, not simply why results were poor.
Question-level analysis is only a starting point, because weak answers on one topic may reflect gaps in knowledge, maths skills or extended writing.
Having staff complete the exam themselves tests whether departmental subject knowledge is strong enough for top grades.
Fifteen or twenty actions overwhelm busy teachers, so the treatment should be two or three sharply focused priorities.
Reviews should ask what the evidence shows rather than who is to blame, ideally with a second leader present to limit bias.
quotes: When I think about what our curriculum leaders in the highest performing subjects do in response to this, their starting point is always the same. They resist jumping straight to solutions. Instead, they build a rich picture of strengths and weaknesses, by looking at performance at different levels:
They don’t use single pieces of evidence when making this diagnosis. Instead they use a variety of evidence sources, gathered over the year, and bring them together:

Once the diagnosis is clear, leaders select the smallest number of very specific actions likely to have the greatest impact clearly targeting the specific issue. The worst possible example of this would be 15-20 actions for teachers to take. With the best will in the world, busy teachers are not going to be able to implement this much change.

The very best curriculum leaders know how to motivate their team to rise to the challenge. They develop a real sense of shared ownership over the challenge of treating the issue and as a result, the whole team feels they are pulling together for the greater good.
This is the stage many departments miss. Leaders often implement changes but do not establish clear success criteria.

At each assessment point, curriculum leaders step back and honestly evaluate how effective the change has been. It’s often best to do this with someone else - maybe a line manager or another curriculum leader, to avoid bias and maintain objectivity.
Keep the cycle going - They treat results analysis as the start of improvement, not the end.
